> **Remote Work and the Future of Cities**
> 
> For much of the twentieth century, the logic of urban growth was straightforward: firms clustered in city centres because proximity reduced the cost of doing business, and workers followed the jobs. This pattern held so consistently that planners rarely questioned it. The pandemic of 2020, however, forced a sudden and unplanned experiment. Millions of employees discovered that a substantial proportion of office work could be performed adequately from home.
> 
> The consequences have been uneven. In some cities, office occupancy has recovered almost entirely, while in others it remains well below pre-pandemic levels. Research conducted across twelve major cities suggests that the decisive factor is not the availability of technology, which is broadly similar everywhere, but the length of the average commute. Where commuting times exceeded roughly forty-five minutes, employees resisted returning; where journeys were shorter, most returned willingly.
> 
> This has produced a paradox. Remote work was expected to empty city centres and revive smaller towns. In practice, the towns that have gained most are those within commuting distance of large cities — places where residents can work from home for three days and travel in for two. Genuinely remote areas have benefited far less, largely because they lack the reliable infrastructure and services that hybrid workers still require.
> 
> Some economists argue that the long-term effect will be a redistribution rather than a reduction of urban activity. Offices may shrink, but the demand for housing, schools and transport in the surrounding region will grow.
